Abstract Trees are an integral component of the urban environment and important for human well-being, adaption measures to climate change and sustainable urban transformation. Understanding the small-scale impacts of urban trees and strategically managing the ecosystem services they provide requires high-resolution information on urban forest structure, which is still scarce. In contrast, there is an abundance of data portraying urban areas and an associated trend towards smart cities and digital twins as analysis platforms. A GIS workflow is presented in this paper that may close this data gap by classifying the urban forest from LiDAR point clouds, detecting and reconstructing individual crowns, and enabling a tree representation within semantic 3D city models. The workflow is designed to provide robust results for point clouds with a density of at least 4 pts/m2 that are widely available. Evaluation was conducted by mapping the urban forest of Dresden (Germany) using a point cloud with 4 pts/m². An object-based data fusion approach is implemented for the classification of the urban forest. A classification accuracy of 95 % for different urban settings is achieved by combining LiDAR with multispectral imagery and a 3D building model. Individual trees are detected by local maxima filtering and crowns are segmented using marker-controlled watershed segmentation. Evaluation highlights the influences of both urban and forest structure on individual tree detection. Substantial differences in detection accuracies are evident between trees along streets (72 %) and structurally more complex tree stands in green areas (31 %), as well as dependencies on tree height and crown diameter. Furthermore, an approach for parameterized reconstruction of tree crowns is presented, which enables efficient and realistic city-wide modeling. The suitability of LiDAR to measure individual tree metrics is illustrated as well as a framework for modeling individual tree crowns via geometric primitives. * Previous * Next Keywords 3D city models Individual crown segmentation Parametric tree modeling Point cloud classification Urban forest inventory 1. Introduction Urban forests are indispensable and provide elementary ecosystem services both directly and indirectly. They regulate urban microclimate through shading und evaporative cooling, mitigate air pollution, reduce urban noise (Rahman et al., 2020, Edmondson et al., 2016, McPhearson, 2011, Nowak and Crane, 2002, Bolund and Hunhammar, 1999), and interact with the built environment by affecting incoming solar radiation and buildings’ energy consumption (Wang et al., 2016, Akbari, 2002). As part of the Urban Green Infrastructure (UGI) they are vital for human well-being and biodiversity, and help achieving the UN Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). The strategic management of urban forests supports a transformation towards more sustainable cities and their adaptation to climate change by providing nature-based solutions (Endreny, 2018, FAO, 2016, Matthews et al., 2015). The calculation of ecosystem service indicators (Derkzen et al., 2015, Gómez-Baggethun et al., 2013) and environmental modeling (Li and Ratti, 2018, Fogl and Moudrý, 2016, Wang and Akbari, 2016) are established approaches to assess the impacts and benefits of urban forests. In studies of urban environments the scope of the analysis and the spatial detail are critical. Urban forests, compromising all trees located in urban and peri-urban areas (FAO, 2016), vary strongly from individual trees to groups of trees and forest patches. The composition of urban forests, the small-scale effects of urban trees, and the high spatial heterogeneity of urban areas result in site-specific differences that have to be considered to derive high-accuracy measurements (Zhao and Sander, 2018). In order to account for site-specific differences, comprehensive and high-resolution data on local scales are needed, which are often lacking (Brzoska and Spāģe, 2020). This data deficit on urban forest structure contrasts with emerging data-rich digital platforms and tools as basis for decision making (United Nations, 2017) and the growing application of 3D city models in urban analysis (Biljecki et al., 2015). Accurate knowledge of urban trees is also a key to developing urban greening plans to increase biodiversity and accessibility of green spaces as imposed by the European Commission with its Biodiversity Strategy for 2030 (European Commission, 2020). LiDAR point clouds from airborne laser scanning (ALS) provide a replicable and scalable way to generate high-resolution, spatially explicit maps of forest structure on a city-wide scale (Alonzo et al., 2016). In allowing the 3D structure of trees to be captured (Vauhkonen et al., 2014), LiDAR point clouds have become the principal data basis for an automated extraction of structural parameters in forestry science (van Leeuwen and Nieuwenhuis, 2010). The widespread availability of LiDAR datasets has led to their increasing use for urban forestry applications (Li et al., 2019). Based on LiDAR, a variety of studies with different objectives can be cited. They range from the identification and mapping of urban forests (Ucar et al., 2018, Höfle et al., 2012, MacFaden et al., 2012) to methods for a segmentation into individual crowns (Xiao et al., 2016, Liu et al., 2013), and the classification of individual tree species (Pu and Landry, 2020, Alonzo et al., 2014). fetched_contents.text: Assessing the potential of multi-seasonal Sentinel-2 satellite imagery combined with airborne LiDAR for urban tree species identification Introduction Urban trees play a crucial role in providing ecosystem services, including purifying the air, alleviating heat in cities, and improving the health and quality of life for humans1,2,3. Effective planning and allocation of urban trees is a nature-based solution for maximizing their benefits and contributing to sustainable urban development4,5. Timely and accurate identification of urban tree species composition and distribution is a crucial prerequisite for the planning and management of urban trees. Accurately obtaining spatial information on urban tree distribution in highly heterogeneous and complex urban environments presents significant challenges. Ground surveys are the most accurate method for collecting urban tree species distribution data. However, this approach is often costly and only suitable for small-scale studies. Integrating ground surveys with remote sensing data is a promising approach for mapping urban tree species6. Compared to ground surveys, remote sensing technology provides observational data at various scales, enabling large-scale, high-precision, and automated classification of urban tree species7,8. Remote sensing-based species identification has been extensively studied in natural environments9,10,11. However, urban environments present additional challenges such as the complexity of land use, diversity of urban tree composition, fragmented spatial layout, and various human-induced pruning and management activities. Some recent studies have already begun attempts in this direction. For example, six tree species were classified in the Grajaú neighborhood of Rio de Janeiro, Brazil, using a fusion of digital aerial imagery and LiDAR data12. In the Greater Chicago Area, 18 common tree species were classified using dense, multi-temporal, high-resolution optical imagery, achieving an overall classification accuracy of 60%13. In the Brussels-Capital Region, the five most common tree species were classified by integrating multi-temporal PlanetScope data with ultra-high-resolution aerial imagery, yielding an OA of 88%14. A decrease in classification accuracy was observed as the number of species categories increased13,14,15. Seven urban tree species within a 100 km² area of Tampa, Florida, were identified by combining multi-season high-resolution Pléiades imagery with airborne LiDAR data16. These studies highlight that optical imagery and LiDAR are the two primary data sources for urban tree species classification. Optical imagery captures the biophysical characteristics of urban tree species, and its spectral, temporal, and spatial resolutions play critical roles in the accurate identification of urban tree species. Spectral differences among species reflect variations in leaf morphology and biochemical factors17. The visible band (VIS, 0.4–0.7 μm) captures differences in the absorption of various plant pigments; the near-infrared radiation spectrum (NIR, 0.7–1.3 μm) reflects differences in internal cell structures of plants; and the shortwave infrared spectrum (SWIR, 1.3–2.5 μm) indicates variations in water content and other biochemical components of vegetation18. Previous studies have identified specific bands important for the classification of urban tree species. For example, the blue light band was identified as significant in the classification of conifer species19. In terms of temporal resolution, different tree species exhibit varying patterns of bud burst, leaf unfolding, and flowering throughout the year, which enhance the separability of tree species based on optical imagery captured at different times20,21,22. Imagery captured during the autumn senescence period provided the most valuable phenological information for tree species classification in Washington, D.C., using multi-temporal WorldView-3 imagery23. In terms of spatial resolution, it is generally believed that higher spatial resolution leads to improved accuracy in tree species classification24,25. However, there generally exists an inverse relationship between the spatial and temporal resolutions of remote sensing imagery, necessitating a comprehensive trade-off analysis for optimal application26,27. It was found that among the optical imagery with 4 m, 8 m, and 30 m spatial resolutions, the best tree species classification results were achieved with an 8 m pixel size28. LiDAR data can capture the biophysical characteristics of urban tree species and serve as an effective complement to optical imagery29,30,31. LiDAR sensors emit thousands of laser pulses and record the time delay between pulse emission and return, creating a 3D point cloud of the imaged area. From the point-cloud data, various tree structure-related features can be derived, such as canopy height, crown width and shape, and leaf area index32. Many studies have investigated the benefits of combining optical imagery with LiDAR point-cloud data for identifying tree species and their compositions. For instance, combining LiDAR data with hyperspectral imagery notably improved the accuracy of identifying urban tree species33. Additionally, fusing optical and LiDAR data increased the average F1-score for classifying urban tree species in tropical regions by 12.6% compared to using optical bands alone12. However, other studies have shown that including LiDAR point-cloud data is not always beneficial. For example, canopy height information had little impact on classification accuracy28. Canopy height information may even cause confusion rather than improve species discrimination34. The reasons behind these phenomena or under which circumstances and for which tree species LiDAR data can effectively improve the classification accuracy, remain unclear. fetched_contents.text: Improving urban tree species classification by deep-learning based fusion of digital aerial images and LiDAR Introduction Urban forests and street trees are essential to maintain and improve human well-being in city centers. They provide various valuable ecosystem services, including air pollution mitigation, carbon sequestration, and surface temperature regulation. Species-specific traits significantly influence the ecosystem services provided by urban trees (Cariñanos et al., 2017). For example, the efficacy of street trees in urban cooling is influenced by their morphological and structural canopy traits, including leaf area index (LAI) (Rahman et al., 2020, Smithers et al., 2018. Similarly, the capacity of urban trees to mitigate air pollution is intrinsically linked to species-specific crown features, such as crown geometry and foliage distribution. These characteristics impact the canopy’s airflow dynamics, potentially increasing the deposition rates of gaseous pollutants and particulate matter (Grote et al., 2016). Therefore, knowledge of the spatial distribution of tree species in urban settings is crucial for understanding and maximizing ecosystem service provision across the city landscape. Ground-based surveys are the most accurate approach to collecting species identity, diversity, and abundance data. However, they are costly, require expert knowledge, and usually only comprise part of the city extent. Integrating ground-based data and remote sensing has been hailed as a promising way to map urban tree species (Shahtahmassebi et al., 2021). Several remote sensing data types acquired by active and passive sensors have been employed (Li et al., 2019). Particularly the use of very high-resolution (ground sampling distance, GSD ≤30 cm) allows identifying individual tree crowns (ITCs) and provides excellent classification accuracy ( > 85%) (e.g., Martins et al., 2021, Zhang and Hu, 2012). Recently, airborne light detection and ranging (LiDAR) data have been employed to improve tree species discrimination (Wang et al., 2018). LiDAR sensors are characterized by their ability to emit tens of thousands of laser pulses, not only in the near-infrared region (with wavelengths approximately 750–1500 nm) but also in the green region (500–550 nm). These sensors record the time delay between the emission of a pulse and its return. LiDAR data is used to construct a three-dimensional (3D) point cloud of the area imaged and accurately measure the height of surface objects. From LiDAR point clouds, one can retrieve species-specific characteristics of ITCs, such as height, crown volume, and shape. LiDAR data alone usually does not provide good results for tree species discrimination. For example, Alonzo et al. (2014) achieved an overall accuracy of 32.9% to classify 29 urban tree species using LiDAR data solely. An overall accuracy value that is significantly lower than the 79.2% achieved using only optical hyperspectral data. Optical-LiDAR fusion is a standard procedure for incorporating LiDAR features to classify tree species. The term ‘fusion’ refers to combining multi-source remote sensing data. Recently, several studies have employed optical-LiDAR fusion to discriminate among species in urban areas (refer to Wang et al. (2018) for a comprehensive review on the topic). Most studies used LiDAR data to incorporate height attributes in the classification process. A few studies explored other LiDAR-derived features, including laser return intensity or surface normals. Intensity showed helpful in reducing the overlap effect between neighboring trees and improving ITC segmentation (Ke et al., 2010). To our knowledge, no previous study employed surface normals to classify tree species. Surface normals from 3D point clouds describe geometric surface properties and can be used to estimate species-specific leaf angle and orientation. A crucial aspect in this context is the need for high-density LiDAR point clouds, which are essential for accurately computing surface normals. While airborne LiDAR data may not consistently achieve the necessary density for precise leaf normal estimation, this limitation highlights a significant research gap. Despite its challenges, the potential of using airborne LiDAR data to classify tree species based on surface normals represents an unexplored area. Another critical issue of LiDAR fusion is related to the fusion approach itself. Most studies rely on an object-based approach in which LiDAR is used to segment ITCs and retrieve a limited number of structural features such as height or intensity. These features are combined with optical-derived spectral features to form a single dataset used by a given classifier to discriminate species. Object-based approaches have limitations because they depend on object segmentation and feature engineering. The former requires using a segmentation algorithm that is usually computationally prohibitive and requires empirical parameter tuning. The latter needs expert knowledge to decide among several image feature extraction approaches, such as texture analysis or color transformations. Convolution neural networks (CNNs) overcome the limitations of object-based approaches by performing feature extraction and species classification in an end-to-end fashion (Kattenborn et al., 2021). In this study, we fused LiDAR-derived features with high-resolution digital aerial images using CNNs to classify tree species in a highly diverse tropical urban area. Our research tested two hypotheses: (i) that surface normals from 3D LiDAR point clouds are sensitive to species-specific differences in crown structural properties, and (ii) that fusing feature maps from encoder-decoder networks trained with optical and LiDAR metrics separately improves the classification accuracy of tree species. Abstract Intelligent management of urban trees is a key issue for Smart Cities, contributing to environmental sustainability and urban well- being. Geospatial technologies and artificial intelligence are increasingly being integrated into smart cites to improve resource management and urban planning. The results demonstrate that PointNet achieves the best overall accuracy of test dataset of 82.07% and a mean per-class accuracy of 70.32%, with competitive performance on Pine (94.37%), Spruce (84.25%), and Maple (86.67%). DGCNN improves the capture of local structures, with 79.15% accuracy in validation, and 67.98% in testing, reflecting slight overfitting. RandLA-Net, although less accurate overall (56.03%), achieves the best inter-species homogeneity (62.32%), and high recall on minority species (Aspen: 86.36%, Linden 85.71%). LiDAR improves urban tree classification by providing direct geometric information that multispectral imagery alone cannot capture. The evidence shows that airborne laser scanning (ALS) point clouds can be used to generate high-resolution, spatially explicit maps of forest structure and that LiDAR is especially useful for capturing tree height, canopy structure, and vertical distribution [N1-F1]. A study on urban forest mapping explicitly states that LiDAR point clouds allow the 3D structure of trees to be captured, and that LiDAR has become the principal data basis for automated extraction of structural parameters in forestry science [N1-F1]. The same study also notes that LiDAR can measure individual tree metrics and supports the reconstruction of tree crowns and semantic 3D city models [N1-F1]. This geometric detail is important for separating trees from buildings and other urban objects, because LiDAR’s 3D point cloud can distinguish vertical structures and height-based objects, making it easier to detect individual trees and crown boundaries [N1-F1].

In practical terms, LiDAR helps separate trees from buildings and other urban features because it provides a 3D representation that can be used to detect local maxima and segment crowns using marker-controlled watershed segmentation [N1-F1]. The evidence also says that LiDAR is used to construct a three-dimensional point cloud of the area imaged and to accurately measure the height of surface objects [N3-F3]. This is particularly helpful in urban settings where buildings, vehicles, and other structures can obscure or confound tree detection. The same source emphasizes that LiDAR-derived features such as height, crown volume, and shape can be used to classify tree species [N3-F3]. In short, LiDAR improves classification by adding vertical and structural context that optical imagery alone cannot provide.

Despite these advantages, LiDAR still has limitations in dense or low-canopy urban settings. The evidence notes that classification accuracy can vary substantially depending on the urban setting, with lower accuracies observed for structurally more complex tree stands in green areas compared to trees along streets [N1-F1]. It also says that tree height and crown diameter influence detection accuracy [N1-F1]. Another source points out that LiDAR data alone usually does not provide good results for tree species discrimination, citing a case where LiDAR-only classification achieved only 32.9% overall accuracy for 29 urban tree species, much lower than the 79.2% achieved using only optical hyperspectral data [N3-F3]. Furthermore, LiDAR fusion studies often rely on object-based approaches that depend on segmentation and feature engineering, which can be computationally prohibitive and require empirical parameter tuning [N3-F3]. In dense urban areas, these limitations can be especially pronounced because occlusions, overlapping crowns, and low-density point clouds can reduce the reliability of LiDAR-derived features [N1-F1][N3-F3]. Thus, LiDAR is strong for height and structure but remains constrained in settings where dense vegetation or low canopy cover makes segmentation and feature extraction less robust.

Multispectral and aerial imagery improve urban tree classification by capturing biophysical properties that are related to species identity and tree health. The evidence states that optical imagery captures the biophysical characteristics of urban tree species and that spectral differences among species reflect variations in leaf morphology and biochemical factors [N2-F2]. It also explains that the visible band captures differences in absorption of various plant pigments, the near-infrared band reflects differences in internal cell structures, and the shortwave infrared band indicates variations in water content and other biochemical components of vegetation [N2-F2]. This means multispectral imagery can detect properties such as leaf water content, pigmentation, and structural characteristics that are useful for species discrimination [N2-F2]. The same source notes that higher spatial resolution can improve accuracy, and that specific bands are important for classification [N2-F2].

The evidence also shows that multispectral imagery can detect tree health properties. A study on WorldView-3 spectral vegetation indices and soil health attributes reports ground-truthed satellite-based urban SVIs, including their relationships with soil health attributes at the individual tree level [N2-R1]. Another source states that for the same tree species, a higher NDVI value indicates a healthier tree, and that leaf size, leaf water content, leaf pigmentation, and stem structure are relevant [N2-R3]. This suggests that multispectral imagery can be used not only to identify species but also to assess condition and health, making it valuable for urban forest management [N2-R1][N2-R3]. Additionally, the evidence says that tree species classification in urban areas is challenging because of the complexity of land use, diversity of tree composition, fragmented spatial layout, and human-induced pruning and management activities, and that optical imagery is critical for accurate identification [N2-F2]. This reinforces the role of multispectral imagery in capturing the phenotypic variation needed for classification in heterogeneous urban environments.

Multispectral imagery also compensates for LiDAR gaps in texture and fine detail. The evidence says that optical imagery can capture the biophysical characteristics of urban tree species and that spectral, temporal, and spatial resolutions play critical roles in accurate identification [N2-F2]. It also notes that optical imagery can provide temporal information through multi-seasonal acquisitions, which can improve separability because different species exhibit varying patterns of bud burst, leaf unfolding, and flowering throughout the year [N2-F2]. The same source mentions that imagery captured during autumn senescence provided the most valuable phenological information for tree species classification in Washington, D.C., using multi-temporal WorldView-3 imagery [N2-F2]. This indicates that multispectral imagery can add fine-grained detail and temporal context that LiDAR alone may miss, particularly when distinguishing species with similar 3D structures but different spectral signatures [N2-F2]. Overall, multispectral/aerial imagery improves classification by providing spectral and phenological information that complements LiDAR’s geometric strengths.

Combining LiDAR with multispectral and aerial imagery introduces several practical trade-offs and implementation barriers. One major barrier is data availability and preprocessing. The evidence explicitly mentions that data preprocessing regroups all steps involved in transforming raw data into a clean, consistent format suitable for deep learning [N5-F4]. It also highlights that multi-sensor fusion techniques require careful preprocessing, including handling raw multispectral and LiDAR data and aligning them into a usable format [N5-F4]. This preprocessing step is important because raw data from different sensors may have different resolutions, formats, and spatial extents, making direct integration challenging [N5-F4]. In addition, the evidence notes that fusion studies often rely on object-based approaches, which depend on segmentation and feature engineering, and that these steps can be computationally prohibitive and require empirical parameter tuning [N3-F3]. This indicates that preprocessing is not a trivial cost but a significant barrier to implementation.

Computational demands are another major concern. The evidence says that optical-LiDAR fusion is a standard procedure for incorporating LiDAR features to classify tree species, and that CNNs overcome the limitations of object-based approaches by performing feature extraction and classification end-to-end [N3-F3]. This implies that fused models often require substantial computational resources because they combine high-resolution imagery with high-density point clouds and may involve deep learning architectures such as CNNs, DGCNN, and RandLA-Net [N3-F3][N5-F4]. The evidence also reports that training and evaluation of deep learning models can be computationally intensive, as seen in a study comparing PointNet, DGCNN, and RandLA-Net for urban tree species classification [N5-F4]. The same source emphasizes that deep learning methods applied directly to unstructured point clouds are most appropriate for tree species classification and outperform traditional feature-based approaches [N5-F4]. This means that fused models may require significant GPU or cloud-based resources, especially when handling large datasets or complex urban scenes.

Sensor integration also affects field deployment and maintenance. The evidence notes that sensor fusion can be used for tasks such as building detection and that LiDAR excels where optical imagery faces limitations, such as dense vegetation canopies [N6-R4]. However, the same evidence also points out that sensor mismatch or alignment problems can reduce fusion value, especially when spectral data is used in decision-level fusion where environmental factors like shadows and occlusions pose challenges [N6-R1]. This means that field deployment is not simply about acquiring data but about ensuring that LiDAR and multispectral/aerial data are properly aligned, calibrated, and synchronized. The evidence further suggests that sensor integration can complicate maintenance because different sensors may have different acquisition schedules, cloud cover requirements, and sensor-specific limitations such as low-density point clouds or limited spectral coverage [N1-F1][N3-F3][N6-R1]. Overall, the practical trade-offs include high preprocessing effort, large computational demands, and deployment/maintenance complexity due to sensor integration and alignment [N5-F4][N3-F3][N6-R1].

The evidence shows that LiDAR can capture 3D structure, tree height, crown volume, and shape, and that it is particularly useful for separating trees from buildings and other urban objects [N1-F1][N3-F3]. It also states that LiDAR point clouds can be used to construct a three-dimensional point cloud of the imaged area and accurately measure the height of surface objects [N3-F3]. This makes LiDAR especially effective in urban settings where buildings, vehicles, and other structures may obscure optical imagery, because LiDAR’s 3D representation can distinguish vertical structures and support individual tree detection [N1-F1]. Another source explicitly states that optical-LiDAR fusion is a standard procedure for incorporating LiDAR features to classify tree species, and that LiDAR-derived features such as height, crown volume, and shape can be used to dis… [N3-F3]. So, LiDAR excels when the goal is structural discrimination, height-based classification, or object separation in complex urban scenes.

Multispectral/aerial imagery is better than LiDAR in situations where species-specific biochemical, phenological, or health-related information is needed. The evidence notes that optical imagery captures biophysical characteristics of tree species, and that spectral differences reflect variations in leaf morphology and biochemical factors [N2-F2]. It also explains that multispectral imagery can detect leaf water content, pigmentation, and stem structure, and that higher NDVI values indicate healthier trees [N2-R3]. The same source emphasizes that optical imagery can provide temporal information through multi-seasonal acquisitions, which can improve separability because different species exhibit varying patterns of bud burst, leaf unfolding, and flowering throughout the year [N2-F2]. In addition, multispectral imagery can provide phenological information from autumn senescence and can be used to assess soil health attributes at the individual tree level [N2-R1]. This means multispectral imagery is better when the classification goal is species discrimination, health assessment, or temporal monitoring, especially in heterogeneous urban environments where spectral variation is more informative than geometric structure alone [N2-F2][N2-R1][N2-R3].

Sensor mismatch or alignment problems can reduce fusion value. The evidence states that environmental factors such as shadows and occlusions in aerial imagery pose further challenges, particularly in decision-level fusion where spectral data may be less reliable [N6-R1]. It also notes that sensor fusion can be used for building detection and that LiDAR excels where optical imagery faces limitations, such as dense vegetation canopies [N6-R4]. However, the same source warns that sensor mismatch or alignment problems can reduce fusion value [N6-R1]. This implies that fusion performance depends on the compatibility of the sensors: if LiDAR and multispectral/aerial data are not properly aligned, registered, or co-registered, the combined information may not improve classification accuracy. The evidence also suggests that different sensors may have different acquisition requirements, cloud cover constraints, and resolution characteristics, which can make integration more difficult [N6-R1]. In short, fusion is most valuable when sensors complement each other, but it can fail when their mismatch or misalignment undermines the ability to combine their strengths [N6-R1][N6-R4].

In short, while fusion is powerful, it also requires careful alignment, preprocessing, and computational investment [N5-F4][N3-F3][N6-R1].

## 6) Sensor-specific complementarity and limitations
LiDAR is better than multispectral/aerial imagery in situations where geometric structure, height, and vertical distribution are critical. The evidence shows that LiDAR can capture 3D structure, tree height, crown volume, and shape, and that it is particularly useful for separating trees from buildings and other urban objects [N1-F1][N3-F3]. It also states that LiDAR point clouds can be used to construct a three-dimensional point cloud of the imaged area and accurately measure the height of surface objects [N3-F3]. This makes LiDAR especially effective in urban settings where buildings, vehicles, and other structures may obscure optical imagery because LiDAR’s 3D representation can distinguish vertical structures and support individual tree detection [N1-F1].

Multispectral/aerial imagery is better than LiDAR in situations where species-specific biochemical, phenological, or health-related information is needed. The evidence notes that optical imagery captures biophysical characteristics of tree species and that spectral differences reflect variations in leaf morphology and biochemical factors [N2-F2]. It also explains that multispectral imagery can detect leaf water content, pigmentation, and stem structure, and that higher NDVI values indicate healthier trees [N2-R3]. The same source emphasizes that optical imagery can provide temporal information through multi-seasonal acquisitions, which can improve separability because different species exhibit varying patterns of bud burst, leaf unfolding, and flowering throughout the year [N2-F2]. In addition, multispectral imagery can provide phenological information from autumn senescence and can be used to assess soil health attributes at the individual tree level [N2-R1]. This means multispectral imagery is better when the classification goal is species discrimination, health assessment, or temporal monitoring, especially in heterogeneous urban environments where spectral variation is more informative than geometric structure alone [N2-F2][N2-R1][N2-R3].

Sensor mismatch or alignment problems can reduce fusion value. The evidence states that environmental factors such as shadows and occlusions in aerial imagery pose further challenges, particularly in decision-level fusion where spectral data may be less reliable [N6-R1]. It also notes that sensor fusion can be used for building detection and that LiDAR excels where optical imagery faces limitations, such as dense vegetation canopies [N6-R4]. However, the same source warns that sensor mismatch or alignment problems can reduce fusion value [N6-R1]. This implies that fusion is most valuable when sensors complement each other, but it can fail when their mismatch or misalignment undermines the ability to combine their strengths [N6-R1][N6-R4].

## 7) Bottom line
In short, combining LiDAR with multispectral and aerial imagery enhances urban tree classification accuracy because the two sensors provide complementary information: LiDAR gives geometric structure and vertical context, while multispectral/aerial imagery provides spectral and phenological detail [N1-F1][N3-F3][N2-F2]. Fusion reduces ambiguity from occlusion, noise, and sensor-specific limitations, and improves robustness across different urban environments [N6-R1][N7][N8]. However, it also introduces practical trade-offs, including data preprocessing, computational demands, and the need for careful sensor alignment and integration [N5-F4][N3-F3][N6-R1]. The evidence therefore supports fusion as a strong but not cost-free strategy for improving accuracy in urban tree classification [N1-F1][N2-F2][N4-R2][N6-R4].
